scope: One original 8-mark AQA AS Chemistry Amount of Substance 3.1.2.5 paper-style application on economic, ethical and environmental advantages of high atom economy; never a flashcard.
notes: Original numerical and discussion task written for the school mock; not a reproduced AQA exam question.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.series: Original AQA AS Amount of Substance Sustainability
questions.question: Atom economy and wider economic, ethical and environmental consequences
questions.subtopic: Evaluating atom economy and process trade-offs
questions.prompt: Two hypothetical routes make sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, as the desired product. Route A: 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(g). Route B: Na₂O(s) + CO₂(g) → Na₂CO₃(s). Relative formula masses: NaHCO₃ = 84.0, Na₂CO₃ = 106.0, Na₂O = 62.0, CO₂ = 44.0. (a) Calculate the percentage atom economy of each route, showing the balanced-equation masses used. (b) Explain one potential economic advantage, one environmental advantage and one ethical advantage of a high-atom-economy route. (c) Explain why atom economy alone cannot show that Route B is better overall. [8 marks]
markPoints: Identifies that Route A consumes two formula units of NaHCO₃, so the total relative mass of reactants is 2 × 84.0 = 168.0.
Uses the desired Na₂CO₃ relative formula mass of 106.0 to calculate Route A atom economy as 106.0/168.0 × 100 = 63.1%.
Uses the total mass 62.0 + 44.0 = 106.0 to calculate Route B atom economy as 106.0/106.0 × 100 = 100%.
Interprets the comparison: Route B puts all reactant atoms into the desired product in the stated equation; Route A also forms CO₂ and H₂O by-products.
Gives a justified potential economic benefit, such as reduced raw-material waste or waste-handling and separation costs per amount of desired product.
Gives a justified potential environmental benefit, such as less material discarded or fewer by-products requiring treatment and disposal.
Gives a justified ethical benefit, for example reduced resource extraction or disposal burdens on affected communities, making clear this is a potential benefit.
Explains that atom economy is a theoretical mass ratio; actual yields, process energy, hazards, sourcing, emissions and costs may differ, so it alone cannot establish which route is preferable.
questions.modelAnswer: Route A uses two NaHCO₃ formula units (2 × 84.0 = 168.0 mass units), so its percentage atom economy for Na₂CO₃ is 106.0/168.0 × 100 = 63.095...% ≈ 63.1%. Route B consumes Na₂O and CO₂ (62.0 + 44.0 = 106.0), so its atom economy is 106.0/106.0 × 100 = 100%. In Route B all the atoms in the stated reactants are incorporated into the desired product; Route A produces CO₂ and H₂O as additional products. Higher atom economy may mean less valuable starting material is converted into unwanted products and lower waste-treatment costs (economic). It may reduce waste and unnecessary raw-material consumption (environmental). Reduced extraction and disposal can also reduce impacts on communities and future resource availability (ethical). These are possible advantages, not guaranteed outcomes: atom economy is calculated from the balanced equation, not experimental yield. Route B could require more energy, costly or hazardous starting materials or have different emissions, so the higher atom economy alone is not enough to choose the better process.
questions.questionType: manually reviewed calculation and evidence-based process evaluation
questions.manualReviewReason: Check both coefficient-weighted atom economies and the separate economic, environmental and ethical explanations. Do not award automatic full marks for keyword overlap or unsupported claims that a route is necessarily greener.
